title: Reviving the Goldkette book and the sound of the bass
summary: He refused to let a modern bassist play four beats in the Goldkette concert, and compares Steve Brown's slap to percussive wooden noises.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: And that's one of the things about that concert that I did. With all that Goldkette stuff, I still have it, but I'm not going to -- I wouldn't go up there and let a guy play four beats on the bass. And I was afraid of that, one of the things I was afraid of, although there were guys like Chauncy Morehouse plays fine two beat music. Ray Bauduc, guys like that, even Davey who went with he can play the Tough when Artie Shaw, was playing four. He was a These are real old timer in two-beat music. But they could give you can get the good rhythms in that. It wasn't just an afterstick. Oo-cha, -- cha, -- cha, it wasn't just a clap like that, you know. It was -- it went along with the arrangement --
Now, even Steve Brown in "My Pretty Girl," he thumps his bass and slaps his bass, but he did it a whole lot
differently than that slapping, wooden type noise that came out of all the guys who figured, 'Well, Steve Brown slaps the bass; I can do that.' And all they were doing was making wooden noises.

And then when I got to the Glen Gray band, for instance, notes didn't mean a thing. It was all percussive boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom - boom, -- din, din, din, din, din, duh-duh, you know. And this is a percussive sound. Guys were taking it way up on the bass fiddle. This takes the bottom out of the band because there's no bass note, no nice bass note; however, the transcriptions, never many got away from that. You listen to the transcriptions, and you hear a nice bit of harmony.
